Abstract. With the rapid development and deployment of machine learning (ML)
and big data technologies, which rely heavily on sensitive user data for training
and inference, ensuring privacy and data security has become a pressing challenge.
Addressing this issue requires methods that safeguard sensitive information while
maintaining the correctness of computational results. Secure multi-party computation
(MPC), as a representative application of cryptographic techniques, offers a technical
solution to this challenge by enabling privacy-preserving computations. It has been
widely applied in scenarios such as cloud-based inference and other privacy-sensitive
tasks. However, MPC also introduces significant performance overhead, thus limiting
its further application. Our analysis reveals that the foundational element of MPC,
the oblivious transfer (OT) protocol collectively account for up to 96.64% of the
execution time. It is because the OT protocols are constrained by low network band-
width and weak compute engines. To address these challenges, we propose POTA, a
high-performance pipelined OT hardware acceleration architecture supporting the
silent OT protocol. In the POTA design, we develop efficient subsystems targeting
the two most compute-intensive parts: the construction of puncturable pseudoran-
dom function (PPRF), and large matrix-vector multiplications under the learning
parity with noise (LPN) assumption within the silent OT protocol. In addition, to
address the performance overhead caused by data transfer between POTA and the
host CPU, we design a host-accelerator execution pipeline to hide the considerable
transmission latency. Furthermore, we design a modular multiplication module over
a finite field to generate the more complex correlations required by MPC protocols.
Finally, we implement a POTA prototype on Xilinx VCU129 FPGAs. Experimental
results demonstrate that under various network settings, POTA achieves significant
speedups, with maximum improvements of 192.57× for basic operations and 597.57×
for convolutional neural networks (CNN).

protecting user privacy have become increasingly prominent. Unlike traditional computing
scenarios, there is a high probability that this private data may be leaked or inferred by
untrusted parties in the process. This issue becomes more prominent with the emergence
of machine learning training and inference services in cloud. Therefore, the protection of
user privacy during computation has emerged as a focal research topic in the realm of
security. As the importance of user data privacy continues to grow, secure computation
services have emerged, such as privacy-preserving training as a service (PTaaS) [WSW+24]
and secure neural network inference as a service (SNNI) [dVM23]. These services heavily
rely on cryptographic primitives and protocols to ensure the confidentiality and integrity
of user data during computation.
As a core area of cryptographic research, secure multi-party computation (MPC)
represents a significant technical approach to addressing security issues in multi-party col-
laborative computation [JX16]. MPC protocols leverage various cryptographic primitives,
such as secret sharing (SS), homomorphic encryption (HE), and oblivious transfer (OT),
to enable secure computation among multiple parties. Under the premise of lacking a
trusted third party, MPC allows parties to collaboratively compute the target functions
using their individual private data, thereby ensuring that the private data of all parties
remains undisclosed, while still obtaining the correct computation results. By employing
advanced cryptographic techniques, MPC guarantees that parties can obtain the correct
computation results without revealing their sensitive input data to others. However, while
safeguarding user data privacy, MPC introduces significant overhead, leading to a drastic
performance degradation in applications. For example, compared to a direct plaintext
multiplication, secret multiplication using MPC protocols may degrade performance by
more than five to six orders of magnitude [ZXWG22]. The cause of bottleneck is that the
MPC protocols introduce a significant amount of cryptographic operations, such as pseudo
random number generation, correlation robust hash function, and modular arithmetic over
finite fields. Despite advancements in CPU instruction sets for cryptographic operations,
they still struggle to meet the performance demands of secure computation in real world,
severely limiting the scalability of MPC applications.
In this paper, we first present four basic operations that are widely used in secure
computation: multiplication, matrix multiplication, bitwise AND, and comparison. These
operations are fundamental building blocks for many privacy-preserving applications,
especially in the domain of ML. Our study is based on the implementation of MP-SPDZ,
which represents the state-of-the-art software MPC framework [Kel20]. We find that up
to 96.64% of the execute time for these operations is consumed by the OT protocols. To
further investigate the performance bottlenecks of OT protocols, we leverage the libOTe
framework [PR], which provides several different classes of OT protocols, to evaluate two
main categories of OT protocols, IKNP-style and silent OT. Our results indicate that the
IKNP-style protocols are constrained by the limited network bandwidth. In addition, while
the silent OT protocol reduces communication overhead, it demands higher computational
resources due to its reliance on more complex cryptographic operations.
Building on these observations and the more realistic network settings, such as 100Mbps
[BCG+19a], we propose POTA, a high-performance pipelined hardware architecture for
accelerating the silent OT protocol. By supporting the silent OT protocol, POTA mitigates
the performance bottleneck caused by limited network bandwidth. Moreover, POTA
mainly involves two subsystems, the construction of puncturable pseudorandom function
(PPRF) and the large matrix-vector multiplication under the learning parity with noise
(LPN) assumption. These two phases are the most compute-intensive parts, which are
implemented as specialized hardware modules tailored to computing requirements of the
silent OT protocol. Ultimately, by enhancing the execution efficiency of OT protocols, the
performance of secure computations is improved.

• We propose POTA, a high-performance hardware accelerator for the silent OT

• In POTA, we develop two novel subsystems specifically targeting the computation-

Background
In Section 2.1, we provide a brief introduction to OT and its variants, followed by an
exploration of the silent OT protocol in Section 2.2. Finally, in Section 2.3, we discuss the
generation schemes of the more complex correlations based on OT.
2.1
OT
The OT protocol is one of the foundational protocols in MPC, initially proposed by Rabin
[Kil88]. Base OT involves the sender sending two messages, m0 and m1, to the receiver.
The receiver, through a selection bit c in {0, 1}, selectively receives one of the messages,
mc. Simultaneously, the sender cannot determine the receiver’s selection bit c, and the
receiver remains unaware of the other message, m1−c. Base OT is also known as 1-out-of-2
OT.
Correlated OT (COT) is a variant of base OT, introduced by Asharov et al. in 2013
[ALSZ13]. The difference from base OT lies in the random correlation between the two
messages. Specifically, the sender inputs a random message m0 and a correlated function
f∆, such as f∆(x0) = ∆+ x0. Consequently, the sent message pair is (m0, m1 = f∆(m0)),
with the receiver inputting a random selection bit c. Similar to base OT, after protocol
execution, the receiver obtains mc while the sender gains no information.
Since base OT protocols are constructed based on various assumptions, such as trapdoor
permutation existence assumption [EGL85], hardness assumption for integer factorization
[Rab05], Diffie-Hellman assumptions [GT08, NP01a], RSA assumptions [LS04, SS05], and
hard lattice problems [PVW08, FYZ11, MM18], it necessitates computationally intensive
public key cryptographic operations [YHW+23]. To mitigate the substantial computational
overhead incurred by these operations, various optimized protocols are proposed, primarily
categorized into the IKNP-style protocols and the silent OT protocols.
The IKNP protocol was initially proposed by Ishai and Kilian in 2003 [IKNP03]. It
first generates κ 1-out-of-2 COT, where κ represents security parameter. And based on
these results, it uses symmetric encryption to eventually achieve m 1-out-of-2 OT. Here, κ
is much smaller than m, and the complexity of symmetric encryption operations is much
lower than that of public key encryption, making its performance superior to base OT.

present the specific implementations of each stage of the silent OT protocol.

Based on the aforementioned analysis, it is evident that improving the efficiency of the
OT protocol can significantly enhance the performance of the MPC applications. However,
the efficiency of the OT protocol is constrained by limited network bandwidth. To address
this issue, Boly proposed the silent OT protocol [BCG+19b]. It requires communication
between parties only during the setup phase, with a communication complexity of O(log N).
During subsequent expand phases, both parties perform computations locally. By reducing
communication overhead and the number of rounds, the silent OT protocol greatly improves
OT efficiency in network-constrained environments. Subsequently, we analyze two OT
protocols, IKNP and the silent OT protocol, and compare their performance under various
network settings. Our analysis leverages the libOTe framework [PR], which offers several
OT protocols, including the aforementioned two. We evaluate the network bandwidth
of these protocols for generating 230 OT instances using the libOTe framework to assess

The results are shown in the Figure 3. We observe that in LAN environment the
network isn’t the performance bottleneck of the IKNP protocol, enabling efficient CPU
computation. However, in WAN environments with restricted networks, the IKNP protocol
not only requires a longer execution time at around 50 Mbit/s network bandwidth, but also
exhibits low CPU utilization, at approximately 3%. This indicates that the constrained
network becomes a performance bottleneck for the IKNP protocol, causing the CPU to
wait extensively for network data transmission or reception. In various network settings,
the network bandwidth demand of the silent OT protocol is comparable, consistently
remaining below 50 Kbit/s over extended periods. Although it only requires lower network
bandwidth, it demands more compute resources, with the CPU utilization consistently
exceeding 10% for extended periods. It is easily concluded that its bottleneck shifts to
computation load, demanding more compute resources than the IKNP protocol, even in
LAN environments.
These findings present an opportunity for accelerating OT. By designing a high per-
formance hardware accelerator supporting the silent OT protocol, we can improve OT
efficiency and secure computation performance. This is primarily attributed to three
reasons: 1) the accelerator supports the silent OT protocol rather than the IKNP protocol,
which heavily relies on network bandwidth. In a real-world environment, achieving high
network bandwidth comparable to LAN is challenging, significantly impacting the efficiency
of an accelerator supporting the IKNP protocol; 2) while network performance is no longer
a bottleneck, as detailed in Section 2.2, the silent OT protocol introduces computationally
intensive operations such as large matrix-vector multiplications under LPN assumption.
Therefore, the accelerator can be designed with dedicated hardware modules to expedite
these operations, further improving the performance of the OT protocol; 3) MPC protocols
primarily use ROT which does not rely on privacy data. We can maximize accelerator
performance by interleaving OT computation and data transmission, thereby hiding the
transmission delays between the accelerator and the host CPU. On the accelerator side,
RAMs are used to buffer output data. On the host side, driver transmit this data to the
running MPC applications.
In real-world environments GPUs are also commonly used to enhance application
performance, particularly for matrix-intensive applications.
However, the operations
involved in the silent OT protocol, such as the construction of PPRF, sparse binary matrix-
vector multiplication under the LPN assumption, and modular multiplication, do not fully
benefit from GPU acceleration. Therefore, GPUs are not suitable for accelerating the
silent OT protocol. In comparison to GPUs, a well-designed FPGA accelerator can more
effectively enhance the efficiency of these operations while also offering lower hardware
costs. As a result, we opt to design a custom FPGA accelerator to accelerate the silent
OT protocol.
4
The POTA Design
Inspired by the above observation, we present POTA, a pipelined hardware acceleration
architecture supporting the silent OT protocol. This section describes how we design POTA

4.1
Architecture Overview
Figure 4 depicts the overall architecture of POTA, comprising two silent OT compute
engines for sender and receiver, along with a 100G Ethernet subsystem and PCIe subsystem.
One silent OT engine serves as the sender in the OT protocol, while the other engine as the
receiver, allowing users to assume different roles. The silent OT protocol compute engine
consists of two subsystems: one for PPRF construction and the other for large matrix-
vector multiplication under the LPN assumption. PPRF utilizes the ChaCha encryption
module as a CSPRNG to generate the GGM tree, which is then saved in Sparse Vector.
The Accumulator and Expander modules achieve the large matrix-vector multiplication
under the LPN assumption, with intermediate results stored in the Sum Vector. With
the outputs from the silent OT protocol compute engine, the OLE/Triple Generator can
generate OLE or multiplication triples. The POTA prototype is implemented on FPGAs.
Therefore, its 100G subsystem is utilized for network communication among parties, while
the PCIe subsystem in the FPGA connects to the host CPU, enabling it to read the
generated OT, OLE, and multiplication triples for the MPC applications.
In the silent OT protocol, the parameter N impacts both the number of OT instances
generated per batch and the hardware resource consumption of POTA. Therefore, we
design N as a reconfigurable parameter to accommodate diverse application requirements
in the future. For applications demanding high security computations and ample hardware
resources such as cloud computing, a larger N can be defined to meet performance demands.
Conversely, there are scenarios where clients have limited resources. However, in MPC
protocols each party must perform secure computations equally, unlike homomorphic
encryption where one party can outsource tasks. In scenarios with an asymmetric client-
server setting, the performance of the MPC protocol depends on the resource-constrained
clients. To address this issue, clients can select a smaller N for limited resources.
Furthermore, we evaluate the security of POTA. We employ the ChaCha encryption
scheme for random number generation, which offers security comparable to AES encryption
scheme [Aum19]. The security of the optimized protocol for large matrix-vector multipli-
cation under LPN assumption has been demonstrated, with detailed specifics available in
[BCG+22]. Overall, in POTA design, hardware acceleration and optimization methods do
not compromise the inherent security of the silent OT protocol, as evidenced in previous

local POTA, this will not lead to privacy breaches for other parties. Furthermore, we
consider side-channel attacks on remote POTA to be extremely challenging and unrealistic.
Therefore, even in the event of a side-channel attack, the security of user privacy data
remains intact.
4.2
PPRF
4.2.1
Design Challenge
As described in Section 2.2, after parties executing the PPRF protocol, they generate a
pair of PCG seeds, which can be extended and constructed into a single-point COT. In the
GGM tree-based PPRF algorithm, the most computationally expensive operation involves
generating cryptographically secure pseudo-random numbers of twice the length, which
needs to be invoked O(N) times. Currently, commonly used CSPRNGs fall into three
categories: block ciphers operating in counter mode, such as AES; cryptographically secure
hash like SHA-256; and secure stream ciphers like ChaCha. Modern CPUs have extended
with specialized hardware instructions for AES, such as X86’s AES-NI [INT24b, INT24a].
Therefore, leveraging its robust AES encryption performance, AES encryption in counter
mode is generally employed as the CSPRNG in MPC protocols.
Despite leveraging CPU-specific hardware instructions to accelerate pseudo random
numbers generation, meeting MPC applications’ performance requirements remains chal-
lenging. For instance, X86’s AES-NI defines two instructions: aesenc performs ShiftRows,
SubBytes, MixColumns, and AddRoundKey operations, equivalent to the first 9 rounds
of AES encryption, while aesenclast executes ShiftRows, SubBytes, and AddRoundKey,
representing the final round. Thus, completing a full AES encryption requires 9 aesenc
and 1 aesenclast instruction. Even with a pipelined AES engine implemented in X86
CPUs, it’s challenging to achieve optimal throughput due to the inability to fully pipeline
AES encryption. A complete AES encryption operation typically requires at least 10 clock
cycles on average, limiting the potential for higher throughput. Additionally, the PPRF
construction approach based on GGM trees requires a length-doubling CSPRNG, where
the length of plaintext and ciphertext in AES encryption are equal. To achieve a length-
doubling CSPRNG, two AES engines with distinct keys can be utilized to concatenate
their ciphertexts as the outputs. However, this approach doubles the hardware resource or
execution time required.
4.2.2
Novel PPRF Hardware Module
To overcome the above challenges, we can choose a more resource-efficient design for the
CSPRNG. This choice is driven by the fact that the proposed acceleration for OT utilizes
dedicated hardware rather than general-purpose processors. Thus, we choose ChaCha

There are two main reasons for using ChaCha encryption scheme to generate pseudo

LPN
4.3.1
Design Challenge
As outlined in Section 2.2, after obtaining multi-point COT, it is necessary to transform
the sparse vector into a random vector based on the LPN assumption, ensuring it remains
indistinguishable from other random vectors. This transformation involves performing
large matrix-vector multiplication between the sparse vector and the parity-check matrix.
Since the parity-check matrix is binary, the addition in matrix-vector multiplication equates
to bitwise XOR operations.
However, it exposes several challenges that need to be appropriately addressed. First,
the size of the parity-check matrix is O(N 2), which requires a substantial amount of
expensive on-chip memory for storage, posing a challenge to limited hardware resources.
Second, due to the simplicity of XOR operations, achieving higher performance necessitates
high memory bandwidth to transmit large parity-check matrices. Finally, large matrix-
vector multiplication is not friendly to pipeline design, making it difficult to achieve higher
bandwidth.

Related Work
Base OT Protocols. The base OT protocol, specifically the 1-out-of-2 OT protocol based
on public-key cryptography, can be constructed under various assumptions. Bellare Mihir et
al. introduced an OT protocol based on non-interactive discrete logarithm problem[BM89].
Additionally, Naor Moni et al. proposed two ROM-based OT protocols[NP01b]. OT proto-
cols presented in [NP01b, PVW08, HL10] are based on the DDH assumption. Apart from
number-theoretic foundations, there are also lattice-based constructions of OT designed to
resist quantum attacks[PVW08, YVV20]. However, whether based on number theory or
lattices, base OT protocols incur significant computational and communication overheads,
failing to meet the performance demands of practical applications.
IKNP-style OT Extension Protocols. Yuval Ishai et al. proposed the IKNP protocol
for achieving m ≫k 1-out-of-2 OT using k 1-out-of-2 OT plus some symmetric encryption
operations[IKNP03]. However, its communication complexity is prohibitively high. To
mitigate this, Gilad Asharov et al. proposed a PRG-based OT extension protocol, and
it requires to execute only a few numbers of base OT protocols[ALSZ13]. The protocol
that halves the communication overhead compared to the IKNP protocol. Kolesnikov
et al.
improved upon the IKNP protocol by enhancing its encoding to extend from
1-out-of-2 to 1-out-of-n OT protocol, known as the KK13 protocol[KK13]. In practical
implementations, Asharov et al. observed that matrix transpose operations consume 43%
of the performance overhead in OT extension protocols. To address this, they employed
the Eklundh algorithm[Ekl72], which reduces the number of swapping costs from O(n2)
to O(n log n), significantly optimizing the performance[ALSZ13]. Regarding CSPRNG,
AES demonstrates efficient hardware support, outperforming typical hash functions by
15× to 50×[GKWY20]. Therefore, these OT extension protocols predominantly utilize
AES with fixed keys as a CSPRNG[YAVV22]. However, despite numerous improvements
in communication, in realistic cloud environments constrained by network bandwidth,
communication remains the performance bottleneck of these protocols.

The silent OT Protocols. Elette Boyle et al. first proposed the framework of the silent
OT protocol, which is based on a novel combination of function secret sharing (FSS) and
noisy linear encodings[BCGI18]. Elette Boyle et al. observed that DPF used as an FSS
scheme is an overkill for the silent OT protocol and can be replaced with the simpler
PPRF primitive, which brings several efficiency advantages[BCG+19a]. Geoffroy Couteau
et al. introduced a variety of candidate new LDPC codes called Silver codes, which
encoding time can be done in linear time and exhibit a large minimum distance[CRR21].
Kang Yang et al. present their technique of COT iterations in a bootstrapped mode. In
this mode, a small portion of resulting COTs from the current iteration are taken as the
refreshed setup COTs that will be used in the next iteration, such that only the first
iteration needs an initial COTs from the one-time setup[YWL+20]. Lawrence Roy put
forward SoftSpokenOT, the first OT extension to improve on IKNP’s communication cost
in the Minicrypt model[Roy22]. Boyle Elette et al. proposed a generator matrix H for
an EA code. It is of the form H = BA, where B ∈Fn×N

7
Conclusion
In this paper, we find that OT protocols accounts for up to 96.64% of the execution time of
MPC applications. To address this challenge, we propose POTA, the first high-performance
pipelined OT hardware acceleration architecture that is not constrained by limited network
bandwidth. One the one hand, we design two novel subsystems for the PPRF construction
and large matrix-vector multiplication under LPN assumption. On the other hand, we
propose execution pipeline among subsystems and between POTA and the host CPU.
Evaluation of the FPGA prototype of POTA demonstrates that under various network
settings, POTA provides up to 192.57× and 597.57× acceleration for basic operations and
convolutional neural networks, respectively.

Abstract: With the rapid development and deployment of machine learning (ML) and big data technologies, which rely heavily on sensitive user data for training and inference, ensuring privacy and data security has become a pressing challenge. Addressing this issue requires methods that safeguard sensitive information while maintaining the correctness of computational results. Secure multi-party computation (MPC), as a representative application of cryptographic techniques, offers a technical solution to this challenge by enabling privacy-preserving computations. It has been widely applied in scenarios such as cloud-based inference and other privacy-sensitive tasks. However, MPC also introduces significant performance overhead, thus limiting its further application. Our analysis reveals that the foundational element of MPC, the oblivious transfer (OT) protocol collectively account for up to 96.64% of the execution time. It is because the OT protocols are constrained by low network band- width and weak compute engines. To address these challenges, we propose POTA, a high-performance pipelined OT hardware acceleration architecture supporting the silent OT protocol. In the POTA design, we develop efficient subsystems targeting the two most compute-intensive parts: the construction of puncturable pseudoran- dom function (PPRF), and large matrix-vector multiplications under the learning parity with noise (LPN) assumption within the silent OT protocol. In addition, to address the performance overhead caused by data transfer between POTA and the host CPU, we design a host-accelerator execution pipeline to hide the considerable transmission latency. Furthermore, we design a modular multiplication module over a finite field to generate the more complex correlations required by MPC protocols. Finally, we implement a POTA prototype on Xilinx VCU129 FPGAs. Experimental results demonstrate that under various network settings, POTA achieves significant speedups, with maximum improvements of 192.57× for basic operations and 597.57× for convolutional neural networks (CNN).
